description: We are a passionate team of Software Engineering and AI enthusiasts who love solving real-world problems through creativity and technology. Our skills include full-stack development, Python, machine learning, data analysis, and UI/UX design. We value teamwork, innovation, and learning. We welcome motivated members with diverse technical and creative skills to build meaningful solutions together.
summary:
FieldVerse is an intelligent, data-driven crop rotation recommendation platform designed to help farmers adapt to climate change, improve soil health, and build sustainable agricultural practices. By integrating NASA Earth observation data, NASA POWER climate records, FAO GAEZ crop suitability information, soil characteristics, and hybrid machine learning, FieldVerse transforms complex environmental data into practical, personalized farming recommendations.

Unlike traditional farming approaches that rely on historical practices or generalized advice, FieldVerse analyzes farmers' locations, crop histories, planting seasons, water availability, soil conditions, and agricultural priorities to generate suitable crop rotation strategies. The platform provides multiple rotation options with crop suitability scores, seasonal planting guidance, expected benefits, potential risks, and clear explanations to support informed decision-making.

With a focus on water conservation, soil health, food security, and climate resilience, FieldVerse makes scientific agricultural insights accessible through a user-friendly platform. By bridging the gap between NASA-powered environmental intelligence and real-world farming decisions, FieldVerse empowers farmers worldwide to make smarter choices, protect natural resources, and build a more sustainable and climate-resilient agricultural future.
details:
What It Does

FieldVerse is a free web app that gives any smallholder farmer in the world a personalised crop-rotation plan for their own field. The farmer pins their location on a map, answers a short form about their crops, water access and priorities, and the app produces three seasonal plans ranked and explained in plain language.

How It Works

The farmer goes through five steps: pin a location, describe current and past crops, describe water access and inputs, give an optional soil-test pH, and set six priorities (water saving, soil health, risk, income, idle land, food). Every question except location has an “I don’t know” option.

The app then shows:

* My Farm — real NASA satellite data for that exact location: monthly rainfall and temperature (NASA POWER), 10-year rainfall trend, vegetation greenness (NASA MODIS NDVI), soil properties (ISRIC SoilGrids), and a NASA GIBS satellite time-lapse.

* Rotation Lab — three 3-season plans compared side by side, each with benefits, risks, evidence citations and what to check locally.

* Climate Time Machine — a “what if” tool: the farmer moves rainfall (−50% to +50%) and temperature (−2 °C to +5 °C) sliders and sees which plans hold up and which don’t.

* Roots of Tomorrow — an animated farm scene above and below ground, driven by real NASA rainfall and real SoilGrids soil data.

* Gap Finder — finds idle months and suggests short crops, cover crops or rest.

* My Plan — a one-page decision card to print or share with a cooperative or extension officer.

* Community — farmers share real experiences with others in the same district.

The Two Analytical Parts

A) Rule-based rotation engine — No global dataset records how crop sequences perform field by field, so we encoded published trial evidence as 13 transparent rules, each cited to 9 sources (including Nature Communications 2025 and 2022, Plant and Soil 2000, FAO and University of Nebraska CropWatch). The engine reads FAO GAEZ v5 crop suitability for 12 crops, builds the site’s climate from NASA POWER and NASA GPM IMERG, checks each crop against rain and temperature limits, scores every 3-season sequence for legume credits and family rotation, and ranks plans by agronomic fit (50%) plus the farmer’s own priorities (50%).

B) ML suitability model — FAO GAEZ is mapped on a coarse 55 km grid, but a farmer’s soil-test pH can differ a lot from the satellite estimate. We trained a scikit-learn HistGradientBoostingRegressor on 85,857 global cells using 33 features: 21 NASA POWER climate features, 7 SoilGrids soil features and 5 location features. The model learns the relationship between soil pH and attainable yield, and adjusts each crop’s suitability when the farmer enters a real pH reading. On held-out test data it reduced the suitability error from 7.4 to 6.6 index points (R² from 0.55 to 0.76) compared with a plain GAEZ lookup.

NASA and Other Data Used

  • NASA POWER (MERRA-2 / SYN1deg) — monthly climate 2001–2020 for model training and the engine; live data for any pinned farm; yearly rainfall 2015–2024
  • NASA GPM IMERG — rainfall variability at 50 reference sites on 7 continents
  • NASA MODIS MOD13Q1 v061 NDVI (via ORNL DAAC) — 250 m vegetation greenness, 2023–2024
  • NASA GIBS (MODIS Terra NDVI monthly) — 12 monthly satellite frames made into time-lapse videos
  • FAO / IIASA GAEZ v5 — crop suitability and attainable yields
  • ISRIC SoilGrids 2.0 — soil pH, texture, organic carbon and nitrogen (CC-BY 4.0)
  • OpenStreetMap and Nominatim — map tiles and place search

All data sources are free and open. No paid APIs are used.

Tools, Languages and Software

  • Languages: TypeScript, Python, HTML/CSS
  • Front end: React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Motion, TanStack Query, React Hook Form, Leaflet, Recharts, Radix UI, i18next
  • Back end: Node.js, Express 5, MongoDB with Mongoose, Zod, Helmet, scrypt password hashing, CSRF protection, rate limiting
  • ML service: Python 3.13, FastAPI, scikit-learn 1.6, pandas, NumPy
  • Testing: Vitest and Supertest (132 unit and integration tests), Playwright (end-to-end browser journeys)
  • Other tools: ffmpeg (NASA GIBS time-lapse videos), Git, GitHub, VS Code
  • AI tools: An AI coding assistant helped write the code. The home page background animation was generated with Google Gemini and is labelled in the app as an illustration, not satellite data.

Creativity

FieldVerse is creative in several specific ways:

  • It uses ML only where real training data exists (crop suitability) and transparent, cited rules where it doesn’t (rotations). Every recommendation can be explained to a farmer in plain language.
  • Climate Time Machine turns static NASA climate numbers into a hands-on “what if” tool — farmers can stress-test a rotation against a drier or hotter future before committing to it.
  • Roots of Tomorrow shows what is happening under the ground using real SoilGrids data and real NASA rainfall — not decoration, but data made visual.
  • Gap Finder turns idle calendar months into productive or soil-protecting time, a dimension most rotation tools ignore.
  • The original farmer mascot “suits up” as an astronaut on login, linking the farmer directly to NASA and space-based Earth observation. All characters, the logo and 11 crop illustrations are original SVG artwork, built in code and released as CC0 (public domain). No stock images or paid assets.
  • The FieldVerse logo shows paddy on one side and soybean, maize and wheat on the other, joined by a gold rotation arrow — the core idea of the app at a glance.

Considerations

  • Farmers often don’t know technical details. Every question except location has “I don’t know”, and the app shows ranges and a lower confidence level instead of guessing.
  • Honesty. No invented data; missing values show as “Not available”; demo examples are clearly labelled; every number states whether it is observed or estimated; every recommendation cites its evidence.
  • Privacy. Coordinates are rounded to ~1 km before leaving the server; Community posts store only the area the farmer chooses (district, province or country), never coordinates; farmers can delete their account.
  • Low connectivity. A low-bandwidth mode skips videos, and plans are printable.
  • Accessibility. Plain language, large touch targets, full keyboard support, calm-motion setting that activates automatically for users who prefer reduced motion.
  • Cost. Only free, open data and open-source software. Free for farmers worldwide.
  • Known limitations, shown in the app. Crop catalogue values still need agronomist review; monthly climate cannot capture short dry spells or frosts; GAEZ cells are about 55 km apart.
